transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Doctor. Well, I'm here because things kind of blew up at work recently. I work in HR, and I basically pushed ahead with this new onboarding launch we were planning. I ended up committing company money and vendor time before any of the actual approvals were in place. 

At the time, it felt... I don't know, it felt bold and completely necessary to just get it done right then. But now I'm on administrative leave, and everyone is asking me what I was thinking. So, that's what brings me in.

Over the past few weeks or months leading up to this incident at work, how would you describe your overall mood? Have you been feeling unusually happy, energetic, or like things are going exceptionally well?

Well, for the past few weeks, it's been a bit of both, honestly. I felt brilliantly alive. I really felt like I could finally show leadership what HR can be, and I was just ready to get things moving. 

But at the same time... I would get suddenly furious if anyone questioned me. Even if it was just over small edits to a document or routine budget questions, I would just snap at them. So, yeah, I felt amazing and energetic, but I also got incredibly angry if anyone tried to slow me down.
Have you ever had a period of time, lasting at least a couple of weeks, when you felt depressed, hopeless, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

No, I don't think so. I mean... I get stressed out, sure, especially in HR with all the employee relations stuff. But feeling hopeless or losing interest in things for weeks at a time? No, I haven't really experienced that. I've always been pretty driven and engaged with my life, so I wouldn't say I've ever gotten down like that.

Is this the first time in your life you've experienced a period like this one—where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, had racing thoughts, or felt like your mind was going faster than normal?

Well, I'm not entirely sure. I mean... I've always been a high-energy person, you know? I get really invested in projects and sometimes work late, but... I don't know if I've ever felt quite like *this* before. Like my brain was just firing on all cylinders and I had to act on everything immediately. So, maybe? But nothing that ever led to me getting put on leave or anything like that.

When you say you've always been a high-energy person and get really invested in projects—have you ever had a time before this recent incident when you felt this same kind of urgency to act immediately, where your thoughts were racing, and you needed very little sleep for several days or more?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had times where I was working hard on a deadline and maybe didn't sleep as much for a night or two, but it wasn't like this. I never had that feeling where my thoughts were just spinning out of control and I felt like I couldn't stop moving. This recent time... it was definitely different. So, no, I haven't had a period like this before.

Looking back over your entire life before this recent incident at work—have you ever had a distinct period, even if it was shorter or less intense than what you're experiencing now, where you felt unusually happy, confident, or on top of the world for several days or longer?

No, I really can't think of anything like that. I mean, I've had good days, obviously, or times when a project went well and I felt proud of my work. But feeling unusually happy or on top of the world for days at a time? No. I've always just been pretty steady, you know? Just focused on getting things done. I haven't had any periods where I felt elevated or anything out of the ordinary like that.
When did this recent period of feeling energetic and needing to act on things immediately actually start? Was it sudden, or did it gradually build up over time?

It wasn't sudden. It... it kind of built up over time. I'd say it's been building for about a month now. It really started right after this new executive came in and started challenging my onboarding redesign. That's when things kind of kicked into high gear, I guess, and I felt like I had to just tackle everything at once. So, yeah, it's been about a month.

Since this energetic period started about a month ago, have you noticed your mood or energy level changing at all—either getting lower or more depressed—at any point during this past month, or has it stayed consistently energetic and elevated the whole time?

No, it hasn't dipped at all. I haven't felt low or depressed or anything like that. It's just been... consistent, I guess. Ever since it started about a month ago, the energy and the drive to just keep going and fix things has stayed right up there the whole time.

During this past month when you've been feeling energetic and driven, have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual—like feeling rested after only 3 or 4 hours of sleep, or not feeling tired even when you haven't slept much?

No, not really. I mean, I'm still sleeping my normal amount. I definitely couldn't run on just three or four hours of sleep. I've been getting my usual... maybe six or seven hours a night. I just wake up ready to get right back to the redesign work. But my actual sleep schedule hasn't really changed.

During this past month, would you say your mood has felt abnormally high or expansive—like you felt unusually confident, grandiose, or like your self-esteem was much higher than it normally is—or has it just felt like normal confidence tied to the work situation?

I wouldn't say it's abnormally high, no. I mean... I feel confident, sure, but that's just because I know what I'm doing with this onboarding program. I've been in HR a long time, so I know my stuff. It's not like I feel grandiose or anything like that. It really just feels like normal confidence. I just know my work is solid, and I feel like I need to defend it and get it implemented now that it's being challenged.

I want to go back to something you mentioned earlier. You said you haven't experienced periods of feeling hopeless or losing interest in things for weeks at a time. But I want to ask more specifically: have you ever had a distinct period—even if it was just a few weeks, or even months—where you felt persistently sad, empty, or down, and during that time you lost interest or pleasure in things you normally enjoy, like hobbies, socializing, or work?

No, I haven't. I mean... I have stressful days at work, sure, but I've never had a period where I felt sad or down for weeks at a time. And I've never lost interest in my work or the things I enjoy doing. It's just not something I've ever really dealt with.

You mentioned earlier that you would get suddenly furious if anyone questioned you during this past month. How much of the time would you say you've been feeling irritable or angry—has that been a constant thing, or does it come and go?

It's been pretty constant over the past few weeks, honestly. I've basically been swinging between feeling brilliantly alive—like I can finally show the leadership team what HR can really be—and getting suddenly furious. If anyone questions me, even over small edits or routine budget stuff, I just snap. It's like I have zero patience for it right now.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a one-month period of elevated mood (feeling 'brilliantly alive'), increased goal-directed activity (impulsive commitment of company resources), irritability when challenged, and inflated confidence in work abilities. While some core manic features are present (elevated mood, increased activity, irritability), the presentation lacks several key diagnostic criteria for bipolar I disorder manic episode: notably absent are decreased need for sleep (patient reports normal 6-7 hours), racing thoughts/flight of ideas (denied), grandiosity (denies abnormally high self-esteem), and psychomotor agitation. The mood elevation and irritability appear partially reactive to workplace stressor (executive challenging her work). The symptom constellation and incomplete manic criteria, combined with the apparent situational trigger, suggest this may represent a hypomanic or mixed episode, or potentially a stress-related mood disturbance rather than a full manic episode. F30.1 (manic episode, moderate) is coded as the primary diagnosis given the functional impairment (administrative leave) and clear behavioral dyscontrol, though the atypical presentation warrants consideration of other diagnoses.
